Suggest null models from what is known about the stressors

Source: R/suggest.R
suggest_null_models.Rd

Applies the guidelines of Schäfer and Piggott (2018, Fig. 3) for the choice of a null model, from what is known about the stressors and their effects: whether the stressors act similarly, whether one of them acts specifically on the physiology of the organisms, whether the effect is mortality, whether the stressor-effect relationship or the distribution of sensitivities is known, how the sensitivities of individuals to the stressors are correlated, and how large the effects of the stressors alone are relative to the effect limit (the largest possible effect, such as 100% mortality or the loss of the whole response). A criterion left unknown (NA) is tried with each of its values, and every null model that one of them leads to is kept: the range of predictions that the authors recommend when the information is lacking, which compare_null_models() then compares.

The result can be given as null_models to estimate_interactions(), which estimates the null models it suggests and keeps the criteria and the reasons in settings$null_model_choice.

Usage

suggest_null_models(
  x = NULL,
  similar_action = NA,
  specific_action = NA,
  mortality = NA,
  stressor_effect = NA,
  sensitivity_distribution = NA,
  correlation = NA,
  effects = NULL,
  near_limit = 0.9,
  level = 0.95,
  response = NULL,
  sensitivity = NULL,
  design = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

A model fitted with fit_responses(), from which the effects of the stressors alone are estimated; a model fitted outside must, with its design, as in estimate_interactions(); the output of describe_design(), to check which null models the design allows; or NULL (the default), to apply only the criteria given.

similar_action

Do the stressors act similarly, with the same mode of action? Schäfer and Piggott (2018) distinguish stressors that act from outside on the whole organism (predation, floods), relatively nonspecifically on its physiology (competition, salinity, heat) and specifically on physiological processes (many toxicants). TRUE, FALSE or NA (unknown, the default).

specific_action

Does one of the stressors act specifically on physiological processes, as many toxicants do? TRUE, FALSE or NA.

mortality

Is the effect mortality? TRUE, FALSE or NA.

stressor_effect

Is the stressor-effect relationship of the stressors known, from earlier studies or from enough levels of each stressor in the experiment (see Details)? TRUE, FALSE or NA.

sensitivity_distribution

Is the distribution of the sensitivities (stress capacities) of the individuals known? TRUE, FALSE or NA.

correlation

How the sensitivities of individuals to the stressors are correlated: "positive" (highly positively: the individuals sensitive to one stressor are sensitive to the other), "negative" (highly negatively: those sensitive to one are tolerant to the other), "weak" (neither) or NA (unknown, the default).

effects

Effects of the stressors alone as proportions of the effect limit: a named numeric vector with one value per stressor, such as c(salinity = 0.3, warming = 0.5). Values cannot exceed 1 (the effect limit); a negative value is a stressor that increases the response, and NA an unknown effect. NULL (the default) estimates them from x when it is a fitted model and leaves them unknown otherwise.

near_limit

Proportion of the effect limit from which the effect of a stressor counts as close to it. Default 0.9 (see Details).

level

Confidence level of the intervals of the effects estimated from x (default 0.95). A criterion that depends on the effects is unknown when an interval spans its threshold; with NULL, the point estimates decide.

response

For a model fitted with fit_responses(), the names of the responses whose effects are estimated; NULL (the default) for all. The other criteria apply to all of them: when they differ (mortality for one response, growth for another), call the function once per response.

sensitivity

As in estimate_interactions(): for a model fitted with fit_responses(), the names of the responses for which an increase means a stronger effect (mortality, damage), whose proportions are then complemented (mortality becomes survival); for a model fitted outside must, TRUE or FALSE. Only used when the effects are estimated.

design

For a model fitted outside must, the output of describe_design() for its data.

data, ...

For a model fitted outside must, as in estimate_interactions(): the data it was fitted to, when emmeans cannot recover them, and further arguments to emmeans::ref_grid().

Value

An object of class must_null_models, a list with:

  • null_models: the codes of the null models kept, for estimate_interactions(null_models = ).

  • models: one row per null model of the guidelines ("AD", "MU", "DO", "SAM", "CA") with its status ("suggested" when it is the only one reached, "possible", or "excluded"), reached (in how many of the evaluations, the contrast sets and times of a fitted model, it is reached), reason (the steps that lead to it, or why it is not reached), design (whether the design allows it: "yes", "no", "some sets", or NA without a design), design_note and note.

  • criteria: the value of each criterion ("yes", "no", a correlation, "below", "above" or "equal" for the sum of the effects, "unknown", "uncertain" when an interval spans the threshold, or "varies" among sets and times) and its source ("given", "estimated" from the fitted model, or "unknown"), with counts in detail when it varies.

  • decisive: for each unknown criterion whose value would change the models kept, the models kept with each of its values.

  • effects: one row per stressor (and response, contrast set and time, for a fitted model) with the effect (estimate), its interval (lower, upper, level, df), its direction, status and reason; for a fitted model, scale says whether the effect is on the response as analysed ("response") or on its complement ("complement", for the proportions described above, which have rows on both scales). NULL when no effects were given or estimated.

  • sets: for a fitted model, one row per response, contrast set and time with the scale to which the guidelines were applied (scale), the type of the effects (on the response as analysed), the sum of the effects and its interval, whether one effect is close to the limit (near_limit), how the sum compares with the effect limit (sum_vs_limit: "below", "above", "equal", or NA if unknown), whether a stressor alone increases the response (increase) and two have opposite effects (opposing), similar_predictions and the null models reached (null_models); NULL otherwise.

  • settings: the thresholds, the source of the effects, the responses whose complement the guidelines were applied to (complement) and the sensitivity with which to estimate the interactions (suggested_sensitivity).

Details

The guidelines. The steps of Fig. 3 of Schäfer and Piggott (2018), in the order in which they are checked; the first whose conditions hold gives the null model:

  1. The stressors act similarly and their stressor-effect relationship is known: concentration addition ("CA"). In must, also with effects of the stressors alone in the same direction (see below).

  2. One stressor acts specifically on physiology, the effect is mortality, and the stressor-effect relationship or the sensitivity distribution is known: the stress addition model ("SAM"). In must, also with no stressor alone that increases the response.

  3. The sensitivities are highly positively correlated, or the effect of one stressor is close to the effect limit: dominance ("DO").

  4. The sensitivities are highly negatively correlated and the sum of the effects is below the effect limit: simple addition ("AD").

  5. The effect is mortality: the multiplicative model ("MU").

  6. The sum of the effects exceeds the effect limit: the multiplicative model ("MU").

  7. Otherwise: simple addition ("AD").

The multiplicative model is the effect addition of ecotoxicology (Bliss independence): "BL" in estimate_interactions() gives the same prediction, with the deviation relative to the reference cell instead of on the log scale. When the mode of action or the correlation of the sensitivities is unknown, the authors suggest computing every null model that matches the remaining criteria; each unknown criterion here takes all its values, and decisive lists those whose value would change the models kept. They also note that the choice matters less when the effect of one stressor is close to the effect limit or about ten times larger than that of the other, since the null models then predict similar joint effects (except perhaps the stress addition model and concentration addition); similar_predictions in sets flags those cases.

The guidelines were written for two stressors and for effects on individuals (or populations, with caveats). For three or more stressors, the same criteria are applied to all the stressors of a contrast set (the effect of any of them close to the limit, the sum of all their effects), and a larger effect counts as about ten times the others when it is at least ten times their sum; dominance is defined in must for two stressors only. Schäfer and Piggott (2018) give no value for an effect close to the effect limit: near_limit = 0.9 is a choice of this package. They suggest at least five levels of a stressor, on an interval or ratio scale, to establish its stressor-effect relationship in a factorial experiment; with a design, models says how many levels of each stressor were tested alone. Concentration addition in must fits its curves to two or more doses, and the stress addition model assumes a beta distribution of the stress capacities (sam_shape in estimate_interactions()).

Effects estimated from a fitted model. For each contrast set and sampling time, the effect of each stressor alone is 1 - y_i / y_0, from the means of the model at the reference cell of the set (y_0) and at the cell with that stressor alone (y_i): the reduction of the response as a share of the reference, whose limit (the loss of the whole response) is 1. The cells with two or more stressors are not used, so that the choice does not depend on the interactions it serves to test. The interval of each effect comes from the delta method on the log scale of y_i / y_0, and that of their sum, the number of stressors minus the sum of the ratios y_i / y_0, on the log scale of that sum, with the covariance and the degrees of freedom that estimate_interactions() uses by default (REML and the small-sample correction). One effect is close to the limit if the lower bound of its interval reaches near_limit, and none is if every upper bound is below it; otherwise the criterion is unknown. The sum of the effects is below the effect limit if the upper bound of its interval is, and above it if the lower bound is. A cell whose mean is fixed at the boundary (only zeros, or only successes) has no variance: the effect of a stressor alone in such a cell gets no interval, and so can take any value up to the effect limit, while the uncertainty of a reference cell at the boundary is left out. Effects are not defined when the mean of the reference cell is zero, when the response takes negative values, or when an increase means a stronger effect in a response that is not a proportion (sensitivity): such a response has no effect limit. The null models kept are those reached in any set and time; sets gives them for each one.

Stressors that increase the response. A stressor, in the sense of Orr et al. (2020) and Madge Pimentel et al. (2025), is any driver of change, whatever its direction: in the 170 studies reanalysed by Piggott et al. (2015), 29% of the pairs of stressors had opposing effects and 22% two positive ones. Each effect of a stressor alone has a direction: "decrease" or "increase" of the response when its interval excludes zero (by its sign for effects given or point estimates), "none" when it includes zero, and "unknown" without an interval. Each set gets the interaction type of Piggott et al. (2015, Table 1) from them: "double negative" (both decrease the response), "double positive", "opposing", "negative neutral", "positive neutral" or "double neutral" ("all" instead of "double" for three or more stressors). The guidelines take the effects with their sign. The sum of the effects exceeds the effect limit exactly when simple addition predicts a response below zero, y_0 (1 - sum of the effects) < 0, so an increase offsets the decreases; only a decrease can be close to the effect limit. Concentration addition treats the stressors as dilutions of one another, which is not possible with opposite effects, and the stress addition model assumes stressors that reduce the response (Liess et al. 2016): steps 1 and 2 also need, in must, effects in the same direction and no stressor alone that increases the response (opposing and increase in sets), as estimate_interactions() already requires for those models. For a proportion fitted with trials that the stressors alone increase and never decrease, the guidelines are applied to its complement (1 - p, mortality for survival), where the increases are reductions towards the limit 0: the mirror of the effect limit for the upper limit 1, which simple addition can also cross, and the scale on which the multiplicative model and dominance describe independent and correlated effects (Madge Pimentel et al. 2025 discuss the asymmetry between survival and mortality). The interactions must then be estimated on that scale: settings$suggested_sensitivity gives the sensitivity for estimate_interactions(), which checks it. For responses of whole communities, such as a total density, some taxa often increase when others are harmed, through interactions among them; the guidelines were written for individuals and populations, and Schäfer and Piggott (2018) point instead to the compositional null model of Thompson et al. (2018), which predicts the community response from the null models of each taxon (not implemented in must).

References

Schäfer, R. B., & Piggott, J. J. (2018). Advancing understanding and prediction in multiple stressor research through a mechanistic basis for null models. Global Change Biology, 24(5), 1817–1826. doi:10.1111/gcb.14073

Liess, M., Foit, K., Knillmann, S., Schäfer, R. B., & Liess, H.-D. (2016). Predicting the synergy of multiple stress effects. Scientific Reports, 6, 32965. doi:10.1038/srep32965

Madge Pimentel, I., Albini, D., Beermann, A. J., Leese, F., Macaulay, S. J., Matthaei, C. D., Orr, J. A., Piggott, J. J., & Schäfer, R. B. (2025). Hypothesis-driven research on multiple stressors: An analytical framework for stressor interactions. Ecology and Evolution, 15, e71959. doi:10.1002/ece3.71959

Orr, J. A., Vinebrooke, R. D., Jackson, M. C., Kroeker, K. J., Kordas, R. L., Mantyka-Pringle, C., Van den Brink, P. J., De Laender, F., Stoks, R., Holmstrup, M., Matthaei, C. D., Monk, W. A., Penk, M. R., Leuzinger, S., Schäfer, R. B., & Piggott, J. J. (2020). Towards a unified study of multiple stressors: Divisions and common goals across research disciplines. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 287, 20200421. doi:10.1098/rspb.2020.0421

Piggott, J. J., Townsend, C. R., & Matthaei, C. D. (2015). Reconceptualizing synergism and antagonism among multiple stressors. Ecology and Evolution, 5(7), 1538–1547. doi:10.1002/ece3.1465

Thompson, P. L., MacLennan, M. M., & Vinebrooke, R. D. (2018). An improved null model for assessing the net effects of multiple stressors on communities. Global Change Biology, 24(1), 517–525. doi:10.1111/gcb.13852

See also

estimate_interactions(), which takes the result as null_models, and compare_null_models(), which compares the null models kept.

Examples

# Two stressors with different modes of action, a nonlethal effect and
# effects of 30% and 50% of the effect limit; the correlation of the
# sensitivities is unknown
suggest_null_models(similar_action = FALSE, mortality = FALSE,
  stressor_effect = FALSE, effects = c(salinity = 0.3, warming = 0.5))
#> <must_null_models> after the guidelines of Schäfer and Piggott (2018), Fig. 3
#> Criteria:
#>   The stressors act similarly (same mode of action)                       no
#>   One stressor acts specifically on physiology                            unknown
#>   The effect is mortality                                                 no
#>   The stressor-effect relationship is known                               no
#>   The sensitivity distribution is known                                   unknown
#>   Correlation of the sensitivities                                        unknown
#>   The effect of one stressor is close to the effect limit (at least 90%)  no
#>   The sum of the effects compared with the effect limit                   below
#>   A stressor alone increases the response                                 no
#>   Stressors alone with opposite effects                                   no
#> Effects of the stressors alone (given): salinity = 0.3 (decrease),
#>   warming = 0.5 (decrease); type: double negative.
#> Null models:
#>   AD (simple addition): possible. Step 4: the sensitivities are highly
#>     negatively correlated and the sum of the effects is below the
#>     effect limit; step 7: none of the earlier steps applies.
#>   MU (multiplicative): excluded. The multiplicative model needs
#>     mortality as the effect (step 5) or the sum of the effects above
#>     the effect limit (step 6), but the effect is not mortality and the
#>     sum of the effects does not exceed the effect limit.
#>   DO (dominance): possible. Step 3: the sensitivities are highly
#>     positively correlated, or the effect of one stressor is close to
#>     the effect limit.
#>   SAM (stress addition): excluded. The stress addition model needs one
#>     stressor that acts specifically on physiology, mortality as the
#>     effect, stressors that do not increase the response and a known
#>     stressor-effect relationship or sensitivity distribution (step 2),
#>     but the effect is not mortality.
#>   CA (concentration addition): excluded. Concentration addition needs
#>     stressors that act similarly, with effects in the same direction,
#>     and a known stressor-effect relationship (step 1), but the
#>     stressors do not act similarly and their stressor-effect
#>     relationship is not known.
#> Unknown criteria that would change the choice:
#>   Correlation of the sensitivities (`correlation`): positive -> DO;
#>     negative -> AD; weak -> AD
#> For estimate_interactions(): null_models = c("AD", "DO")
# The same, with an effect close to the effect limit
suggest_null_models(similar_action = FALSE, mortality = FALSE,
  stressor_effect = FALSE, effects = c(salinity = 0.3, warming = 0.95))
#> <must_null_models> after the guidelines of Schäfer and Piggott (2018), Fig. 3
#> Criteria:
#>   The stressors act similarly (same mode of action)                       no
#>   One stressor acts specifically on physiology                            unknown
#>   The effect is mortality                                                 no
#>   The stressor-effect relationship is known                               no
#>   The sensitivity distribution is known                                   unknown
#>   Correlation of the sensitivities                                        unknown
#>   The effect of one stressor is close to the effect limit (at least 90%)  yes
#>   The sum of the effects compared with the effect limit                   above
#>   A stressor alone increases the response                                 no
#>   Stressors alone with opposite effects                                   no
#> Effects of the stressors alone (given): salinity = 0.30 (decrease),
#>   warming = 0.95 (decrease); type: double negative.
#> Null models:
#>   AD (simple addition): excluded. Not reached: an earlier step always
#>     applies (step 3, dominance).
#>   MU (multiplicative): excluded. Not reached: an earlier step always
#>     applies (step 3, dominance).
#>   DO (dominance): suggested. Step 3: the sensitivities are highly
#>     positively correlated, or the effect of one stressor is close to
#>     the effect limit.
#>   SAM (stress addition): excluded. The stress addition model needs one
#>     stressor that acts specifically on physiology, mortality as the
#>     effect, stressors that do not increase the response and a known
#>     stressor-effect relationship or sensitivity distribution (step 2),
#>     but the effect is not mortality.
#>   CA (concentration addition): excluded. Concentration addition needs
#>     stressors that act similarly, with effects in the same direction,
#>     and a known stressor-effect relationship (step 1), but the
#>     stressors do not act similarly and their stressor-effect
#>     relationship is not known.
#> For estimate_interactions(): null_models = "DO"

# Effects estimated from a fitted model
jars <- expand.grid(
  salinity = c("ambient", "high"),
  warming = c("no", "yes"),
  replicate = 1:5,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
jars$jar <- seq_len(nrow(jars))
mu <- 40 * ifelse(jars$salinity == "high", 0.5, 1) *
  ifelse(jars$warming == "yes", 0.4, 1)
jars$algae <- stats::qpois(c(0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8)[jars$replicate], mu)
design <- describe_design(jars, c("salinity", "warming"),
  control = c(salinity = "ambient", warming = "no"), unit = "jar")
fits <- fit_responses(jars, "algae", design, residual_checks = FALSE,
  seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
choice <- suggest_null_models(fits, similar_action = FALSE, mortality = FALSE,
  stressor_effect = FALSE)
choice
#> <must_null_models> after the guidelines of Schäfer and Piggott (2018), Fig. 3
#> Criteria:
#>   The stressors act similarly (same mode of action)                       no
#>   One stressor acts specifically on physiology                            unknown
#>   The effect is mortality                                                 no
#>   The stressor-effect relationship is known                               no
#>   The sensitivity distribution is known                                   unknown
#>   Correlation of the sensitivities                                        unknown
#>   The effect of one stressor is close to the effect limit (at least 90%)  no (estimated)
#>   The sum of the effects compared with the effect limit                   uncertain (estimated; an interval spans the threshold)
#>   A stressor alone increases the response                                 no (estimated)
#>   Stressors alone with opposite effects                                   no (estimated)
#> Effects of the stressors alone: estimated in 1 of 1 contrast sets and
#>   times, with 95% intervals.
#>   Directions of the effects (types of Piggott et al. 2015): double
#>   negative in 1.
#> Null models:
#>   AD (simple addition): possible. Step 4: the sensitivities are highly
#>     negatively correlated and the sum of the effects is below the
#>     effect limit; step 7: none of the earlier steps applies.
#>   MU (multiplicative): possible. Step 6: the sum of the effects exceeds
#>     the effect limit. The effect addition of ecotoxicology: "BL" (Bliss
#>     independence) gives the same prediction, with the deviation
#>     relative to the reference cell.
#>   DO (dominance): possible. Step 3: the sensitivities are highly
#>     positively correlated, or the effect of one stressor is close to
#>     the effect limit.
#>   SAM (stress addition): excluded. The stress addition model needs one
#>     stressor that acts specifically on physiology, mortality as the
#>     effect, stressors that do not increase the response and a known
#>     stressor-effect relationship or sensitivity distribution (step 2),
#>     but the effect is not mortality.
#>   CA (concentration addition): excluded. Concentration addition needs
#>     stressors that act similarly, with effects in the same direction,
#>     and a known stressor-effect relationship (step 1), but the
#>     stressors do not act similarly and their stressor-effect
#>     relationship is not known.
#> Unknown criteria that would change the choice:
#>   Correlation of the sensitivities (`correlation`): positive -> DO;
#>     negative -> AD, MU; weak -> AD, MU
#>   Sum of the effects vs the limit (`sum`): below -> AD, DO; above ->
#>     MU, DO
#> For estimate_interactions(): null_models = c("AD", "MU", "DO")
choice$effects[, c("stressor", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
#>   stressor  estimate     lower     upper
#> 1 salinity 0.4974874 0.3610238 0.6048071
#> 2  warming 0.6030151 0.4848120 0.6940980
# The null models kept, with their justification in the settings
est <- estimate_interactions(fits, null_models = choice, n_sim = 2000, seed = 1)
est$settings$null_model_choice$criteria
#>                   criterion
#> 1            similar_action
#> 2           specific_action
#> 3                 mortality
#> 4           stressor_effect
#> 5  sensitivity_distribution
#> 6               correlation
#> 7                near_limit
#> 8                       sum
#> 9                  increase
#> 10                 opposing
#>                                                                  question
#> 1                       The stressors act similarly (same mode of action)
#> 2                            One stressor acts specifically on physiology
#> 3                                                 The effect is mortality
#> 4                               The stressor-effect relationship is known
#> 5                                   The sensitivity distribution is known
#> 6                                        Correlation of the sensitivities
#> 7  The effect of one stressor is close to the effect limit (at least 90%)
#> 8                   The sum of the effects compared with the effect limit
#> 9                                 A stressor alone increases the response
#> 10                                  Stressors alone with opposite effects
#>        value    source detail
#> 1         no     given       
#> 2    unknown   unknown       
#> 3         no     given       
#> 4         no     given
